content.value:
Your starter file has a working PID turn-to-heading controller already wired up. When you press START, the robot turns to face 90 degrees.

A PID controller is a feedback loop: it measures the current heading, compares it to a target, and corrects the difference. It does this dozens of times per second, always steering toward the target.

That is the whole idea — measure, compare, correct. PID is just a smart way to decide how much to correct each time.

Run it now and watch the robot turn and settle on 90 degrees. Your job is to understand why it works, then tune the three constants.

steps.title: Error: how far off we are

content.value:
Every correction starts with error — the gap between where we are and where we want to be.

If the target is 90 degrees and the robot faces 0, the error is 90. If it faces 170, the error is negative — it needs to turn left.

One subtlety: heading wraps around. If you are at 170 and the target is -170, the true error is only 20 degrees, not 340. The controller always takes the shortest turn.

Everything after this is just three different ways of turning that error into a motor command.

The P term corrects in proportion to the error. Big error, big correction. Small error, small correction.

Far from the target, the robot pushes hard. As it gets close, it eases off. This is the main term — it does most of the work.

Turn kP up too high and the robot overshoots and oscillates. Too low and it reacts weakly. P alone usually cannot finish the job: it leaves a small lingering error.

The I term accumulates error over time. It looks at how long you have been off target and keeps adding up that error.

This fixes the lingering error that P leaves behind. If the robot is stuck 2 degrees off and P is too weak to move it, the integral grows until the correction is strong enough to push through.

The risk is windup — the accumulated sum keeps growing and overshoots. A good controller resets the integral when you cross the target.

The D term reacts to how fast the error is changing — the trend, not the amount.

If the robot is closing in quickly, D applies a braking force so it does not overshoot. It damps the motion and smooths out what P wants to do.

Too much D makes the approach sluggish. Too little lets the robot bounce past the target.

Now tune the constants:

1. Set kI = 0 and kD = 0. Raise kP until the robot oscillates around the target, then back off to about 70% of that.

2. Raise kD until the overshoot disappears and the robot settles cleanly.

3. Raise kI just enough to wipe out any remaining steady-state error.

The robot should settle within 2 degrees of target in under 1.5 seconds.

This is the same PID that SolversLib uses under the hood — setVeloCoefficients(kP, kI, kD) on a Motor configures exactly these three terms.
